study.title: Joshua 20 - The cities of refuge and the protection of justice
study.overview: This chapter formalizes the designation of cities of refuge in Israel. The text resumes the instruction already given through Moses and shows that Joshua, with the leadership of the people, separates specific cities to protect who killed someone without intention. The purpose is not to cover up guilt, but to prevent accidental death from being treated as premeditated homicide before proper judgment. The chapter concludes by emphasizing that this protection also reached the resident foreigner, showing that God's justice should be valid for all those who lived among the people.

outline.title: Divine Order and purpose of cities
outline.explanation: The LORD guides Joshua to instruct Israel to separate cities of refuge. The target is to welcome the involuntary homicide, that is, who killed it without intention, protecting him from the avenger of the dead until the case is evaluated.

outline.title: Procedure of reception and permanence
outline.explanation: Whoever sought refuge should expose his cause to the gate of the city. If the elders received him, he would live there until the community judgment and until the death of the great priest of that time, when he could return to his city.

outline.title: The chosen cities and the universal range of protection
outline.explanation: Six cities are designated: three to the west and three to the east of the Jordan. The text concludes by stating that the provision served all Israelis and also the resident foreigner, without distinction as to the involuntary accident.

study.context: The chapter is linked to the previous instructions given by Moses about cities of refuge and now shows its realization on the already distributed land. The notes highlight that this occurred before the land was fully distributed and that the cities chosen were well distributed throughout the territory, in a practical and accessible way. The text also preserves the social reality of the avenger of the dead, a legal figure recognized in the Israeli system itself.
study.theology: Chapter theology combines justice, mercy and community order. First, it carefully distinguishes between intentional homicide and accidental death; the law does not treat all bloodshed in the same way. Second, it limits private revenge, preventing the immediate reaction from replacing the trial. Third, it shows that divine protection involves institutional mediation: elders, judgment and the role of the great priest appear as part of the process. Finally, the inclusion of the resident foreigner reveals that God's provision was not ethnic privilege, but an expression of justice for all who were under the common life of Israel. Typological reading appears in commentators as a figure of God's provision in favor of those seeking shelter, but this should be treated as interpretation, not as a unique mandatory sense of the text.

scholarViews.insight: The cities of refuge were an important advance in human relations, and the resident foreigner received the same justice as the native Israeli.
The appointment of cities in the territory of Canaan was made with the authority of Joshua and the leaders, reaffirming and concluding the s of these cities of refuge.
The cities were distributed at adequate distances to be accessible to any part of the country, and also the foreigner was entitled to the same benefit.

questions: Why did God demand that the case of the involuntary homicide be judged before any definitive punishment?
What does the presence of the avenger of the dead reveal about the tension between family justice and public justice in Israel?
How does the inclusion of the resident foreigner challenge limited views of whom it deserves legal protection?
study.practice: This chapter calls the community of faith to take justice seriously without erasing mercy. In practice, this means avoiding hasty judgments, listening to circumstances carefully and protecting vulnerable people until the truth is examined. It also challenges the church to treat the foreigner, the migrant and the different with the same dignity granted to the members of the group, remembering that biblical justice does not favor only those from within. Moreover, the figure of refuge invites the believer to trust in God as a shelter in situations of guilt, fear and need for protection.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are in the form of excerpts, and that of Matthew Henry appears truncated in the material received. Therefore, some interpretive nuances of it cannot be developed safely. It is also not possible to state more than the text itself and the notes say about historical details, such as exact dates, broad geography or practices not explicitly mentioned here.
